subtopics.title: computer components
subtopics.teaching: A computer system uses components such as the processor, memory, storage, motherboard and power system, each serving a different role.
subtopics.worked_example: RAM temporarily holds data and instructions being actively used, while storage retains files when power is off.
subtopics.pitfall: More storage capacity does not mean more processing speed.
subtopics.mastery: Explain the role of major computer components and distinguish temporary memory from persistent storage.

subtopics.title: input output and storage
subtopics.teaching: Input devices send information to a computer; output devices present results; storage keeps data for later use.
subtopics.worked_example: A keyboard is an input device, a monitor is an output device, and an SSD is storage.
subtopics.pitfall: A touchscreen can provide both input and output because it displays information and detects touch.
subtopics.mastery: Classify devices by their primary functions and recognize devices with multiple roles.

subtopics.title: operating systems
subtopics.teaching: An operating system manages hardware resources and provides services that allow applications to run and users to interact with the device.
subtopics.worked_example: A file manager, process scheduler and device drivers are examples of functions associated with operating systems.
subtopics.pitfall: An application such as a word processor is not itself the operating system.
subtopics.mastery: Describe what an operating system does and distinguish system software from application software.

subtopics.title: files and folders
subtopics.teaching: Files store information while folders organize files and other folders into a manageable structure.
subtopics.worked_example: Placing photos inside a named folder and using meaningful filenames makes retrieval easier.
subtopics.pitfall: Renaming a file does not automatically change its contents.
subtopics.mastery: Organize files using sensible names, folders and extensions while understanding basic file operations.

subtopics.title: digital devices
subtopics.teaching: Digital devices process information electronically and include computers, smartphones, tablets, cameras and many embedded systems.
subtopics.worked_example: A smart thermostat is a computing device because it senses information, processes it and controls an output.
subtopics.pitfall: A device does not need a keyboard or screen to contain computing capability.
subtopics.mastery: Identify computing devices and explain their input-process-output behaviour.

subtopics.title: web browsers and search
subtopics.teaching: A browser retrieves and displays web resources, while a search engine helps locate indexed information by query.
subtopics.worked_example: Typing a question into a search engine produces results; opening one result then uses a browser to request the webpage.
subtopics.pitfall: A search engine and browser are different tools even though they are commonly used together.
subtopics.mastery: Distinguish browser functions from search-engine functions and formulate useful searches.

subtopics.title: network basics
subtopics.teaching: A network connects devices so they can exchange data and share resources; local and wide-area networks differ in scale and scope.
subtopics.worked_example: Devices on a home network may communicate through a router, while the internet connects networks across the world.
subtopics.pitfall: The internet is not a single cable or single computer.
subtopics.mastery: Explain basic network roles and distinguish a local network from the internet.

subtopics.title: URLs and domains
subtopics.teaching: A URL identifies the location and access method of a web resource; a domain is the human-readable name within an internet addressing system.
subtopics.worked_example: In a URL such as https://example.com/page, the scheme is https, the domain is example.com and /page identifies a resource path.
subtopics.pitfall: A domain name is not the same thing as the entire URL.
subtopics.mastery: Identify major URL parts and use domains as one signal when evaluating a destination.

subtopics.title: connectivity
subtopics.teaching: Connectivity depends on technologies such as Wi-Fi, mobile networks, Ethernet and Bluetooth, each suited to different ranges and uses.
subtopics.worked_example: A phone may use Wi-Fi for a home connection and mobile data when away from that network.
subtopics.pitfall: A device being connected to Wi-Fi does not guarantee that the internet service itself is available.
subtopics.mastery: Choose appropriate connectivity methods and distinguish local connection from internet access.

subtopics.title: online communication
subtopics.teaching: Online communication includes email, messaging, video meetings, forums and collaborative platforms, each with different audience and persistence characteristics.
subtopics.worked_example: A formal school email should use an appropriate subject and respectful wording, while a quick message to a friend can be shorter.
subtopics.pitfall: Digital communication can be copied or forwarded beyond its original audience.
subtopics.mastery: Select suitable channels and communicate clearly with awareness of audience and permanence.

subtopics.title: passwords and authentication
subtopics.teaching: Authentication verifies identity. Strong unique passwords, password managers and multi-factor authentication reduce account compromise risk.
subtopics.worked_example: A unique password for an important account plus a second authentication factor provides stronger protection than reusing one password everywhere.
subtopics.pitfall: A password that is merely long but reused across sites can expose multiple accounts after one breach.
subtopics.mastery: Create and evaluate safer authentication practices without sharing secrets.

subtopics.title: privacy and personal data
subtopics.teaching: Personal data can include names, contact details, identifiers, location information, photos and account information. Privacy controls limit unnecessary exposure.
subtopics.worked_example: Before posting a location-tagged photo, consider whether the location and metadata reveal information that should remain private.
subtopics.pitfall: Publicly available does not mean harmless or impossible to misuse.
subtopics.mastery: Identify sensitive information and choose appropriate sharing and privacy settings.

subtopics.title: phishing and scams
subtopics.teaching: Phishing attempts trick people into revealing information or taking unsafe actions through deceptive messages, websites or calls.
subtopics.worked_example: An urgent message demanding a password reset through an unfamiliar link is a warning sign; verify through the service's official channel instead.
subtopics.pitfall: A familiar logo or convincing wording does not prove that a message is genuine.
subtopics.mastery: Spot common warning signs and verify requests independently before acting.

subtopics.title: device security
subtopics.teaching: Device security includes updates, screen locks, trusted software, backups and careful handling of removable media or downloads.
subtopics.worked_example: Installing security updates and using an automatic screen lock reduce common attack opportunities.
subtopics.pitfall: Security software cannot compensate for every unsafe user action.
subtopics.mastery: Apply layered device-security practices and explain why each layer matters.

subtopics.title: digital citizenship
subtopics.teaching: Digital citizenship involves responsible, respectful and safe participation in digital environments, including respecting others, intellectual property and community rules.
subtopics.worked_example: Before reposting a claim about someone, check its source and consider the potential harm of spreading it.
subtopics.pitfall: Being online does not remove responsibilities that apply offline.
subtopics.mastery: Make responsible choices about communication, attribution, consent and online behaviour.

subtopics.title: documents
subtopics.teaching: Document software supports structured text creation through formatting, headings, tables, lists and revision features.
subtopics.worked_example: Using heading styles makes a long report easier to navigate and can support automatic tables of contents.
subtopics.pitfall: Changing font size manually for every heading is less consistent than using styles.
subtopics.mastery: Create clear structured documents using appropriate formatting and organization.

subtopics.title: spreadsheets
subtopics.teaching: Spreadsheets organize data in cells and can calculate results using formulas and functions.
subtopics.worked_example: If B2 contains quantity and C2 contains price, =B2*C2 calculates the row total rather than requiring manual arithmetic.
subtopics.pitfall: Typing calculated totals manually makes updates error-prone.
subtopics.mastery: Use cell references, formulas and basic functions to analyse structured data.

subtopics.title: presentations
subtopics.teaching: Effective presentations combine concise text, meaningful visuals and logical sequencing for an audience; slides should support rather than replace explanation.
subtopics.worked_example: A slide showing three key findings with a simple chart is easier to follow than a paragraph containing every detail.
subtopics.pitfall: Adding animations or decorative elements does not automatically improve communication.
subtopics.mastery: Design readable slides with clear hierarchy and audience-appropriate content.

subtopics.title: search strategies
subtopics.teaching: Search quality improves when queries use specific terms, useful phrases, filters and alternative keywords instead of vague wording.
subtopics.worked_example: Searching 'water cycle evaporation condensation precipitation' is more targeted than searching only 'water'.
subtopics.pitfall: More words are not always better if irrelevant terms obscure the goal.
subtopics.mastery: Refine searches iteratively and use terms that represent the information need.

subtopics.title: source evaluation
subtopics.teaching: Reliable information should be assessed for authorship, evidence, date, purpose, relevance and agreement with other credible sources.
subtopics.worked_example: A page that provides an identifiable author, supporting references and a recent publication date may be stronger evidence than an anonymous unsourced post.
subtopics.pitfall: A polished website design is not proof of reliability.
subtopics.mastery: Evaluate sources using evidence and provenance rather than appearance alone.

subtopics.title: algorithms
subtopics.teaching: An algorithm is a finite, ordered set of instructions for solving a problem or completing a task.
subtopics.worked_example: To find the larger of two numbers, compare them and output the one that is greater; this is an algorithm independent of programming language.
subtopics.pitfall: A list of instructions can still be ambiguous if steps are not precise.
subtopics.mastery: Write ordered, unambiguous steps with clear inputs and outputs.

subtopics.title: variables
subtopics.teaching: A variable is a named storage location or symbolic reference whose value can be used and changed during computation.
subtopics.worked_example: If score starts at 0 and later becomes 10, the variable score holds the current value used by the program.
subtopics.pitfall: A variable name describes a value but is not necessarily the value itself.
subtopics.mastery: Trace variable values through a sequence of assignments.

subtopics.title: conditions
subtopics.teaching: Conditional logic chooses actions based on whether a Boolean expression is true or false.
subtopics.worked_example: If temperature > 30, a program might display 'hot'; otherwise it displays 'not hot'.
subtopics.pitfall: A condition must be evaluated before deciding which branch executes.
subtopics.mastery: Construct and trace if/else decisions using clear Boolean conditions.

subtopics.title: loops
subtopics.teaching: Loops repeat instructions while a condition or collection requires further processing, reducing unnecessary duplicate code.
subtopics.worked_example: A loop can add the numbers 1 through 5 without writing five separate addition statements.
subtopics.pitfall: An incorrectly designed loop can run forever or repeat the wrong number of times.
subtopics.mastery: Identify initialization, condition, update and repeated body when tracing loops.

subtopics.title: debugging
subtopics.teaching: Debugging is the systematic process of finding and correcting faults in a program by reproducing, isolating and testing problems.
subtopics.worked_example: If a loop produces six outputs instead of five, inspect its starting value, stopping condition and update step.
subtopics.pitfall: Changing several unrelated lines at once makes the source of a fix harder to identify.
subtopics.mastery: Use evidence, small changes and retesting to locate and fix bugs.

subtopics.title: decomposition
subtopics.teaching: Learn decomposition as a core Computational Thinking competency in Computer Challenge. Build the underlying concept, then practise recognition, application, error detection and transfer to unfamiliar questions. Students should explain the reasoning, distinguish strong evidence from distractors, and verify the answer against the wording and constraints.
subtopics.worked_example: Worked example: apply decomposition to a representative problem, identify the decisive clue or rule, work through the reasoning, and verify the result.
subtopics.pitfall: Common pitfall: selecting a familiar-looking answer without checking the exact wording, relationship, sequence, evidence or constraint required by the question.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: solve an unfamiliar decomposition task independently, explain the reasoning, reject a plausible distractor with evidence, and verify the final answer.
